text: Lesson 7 proved the backup-and-restore mechanism actually works. This lesson is smaller and faster: a quick, repeatable check anyone covering for a DBA can run to answer, is this database okay right now, without waiting for an incident to find out.

The first half is a real DMV query. sys.dm_exec_sessions is a real-time dynamic management view, one row per authenticated session, showing who's logged in, from where, and how much CPU and memory that session has used. Filtering to is_user_process equals 1 drops SQL Server's own internal system sessions, so you're only looking at real activity — the scheduling app, the billing app, anyone connected directly.

At a glance, this answers two practical questions: is anything actually connected — zero sessions during business hours could itself be a sign something's wrong upstream — and does anything look abnormal, like one session consuming far more CPU than the rest.

The second half reuses a signal you already know: checking earliestRestoreDate again, the same way you did in Lessons 4 through 6, to confirm the automated backup chain is still current. A recent, moving value means a healthy chain. A stale or missing one is the first sign something's wrong with backups, worth catching long before it becomes Lesson 1's scenario all over again.

This is deliberately a basic check — one query and one command, not a full monitoring dashboard, because that's a different project from what was actually asked. Next lesson, this check and everything else you've built gets written down as a real runbook.
